title: Input fingerprints improved task prediction and joint structure improved spike prediction in 176 IBL regions
abstract: We tested prediction of five task scores and nine intrinsic spike measures in 176 IBL brain regions. Input fingerprints used the Knox connectome. Neuron-type composition used Allen MERFISH. Nested kernel ridge models compared geometry and division with added input, types, or both. Five random and five spatial partitions kept test physiology out of training and tuning. With a 1 mm geometry kernel, spatial task error fell from 1.0636 to 0.8719 with input, versus 1.0203 with types. Spatial intrinsic error fell from 1.2026 to 0.9231 with both, versus 1.0372 with input and 1.0186 with types. The combined intrinsic model beat both single additions in every partition at geometry lengths 0.5, 1 and 2 mm. The better single intrinsic addition changed with geometry length. Input gave a larger mean task gain than types in every tested length and split design. These results support task prediction from input and intrinsic prediction from joint structure. They do not establish a strict causal split. Existing region averages, repeated and partly identical partitions, fixed kernel weights, anatomy and recording confounds, and unequal reliability limit inference. Code, aggregate scores, a figure, exact input hashes and external regeneration steps are included. Source matrices and individual predictions are excluded.

display.caption: Gain over geometry and division for five task and nine intrinsic measures in 176 regions. Dots show five partitions of the same sample. They are not independent experiments. Spatial intrinsic prediction was best with both input and cell types.
